identification.summary: Unfading Sea Haze is a name given by Bitdefender Labs to a previously unreported threat actor that attacked high-level, mainly military and government organizations in South China Sea countries; Bitdefender's investigation found at least eight victims and reached back to 2018 [S1][S3]. The name reflects the group's persistence and regional focus, and Bitdefender found no clear link to any previously identified actor, which is why it assigned a new name [S1][S3]. Bitdefender judged the actor to be Chinese-aligned on circumstantial evidence [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least 2018, per Bitdefender's investigation (reported May 2024) [S1][S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name and no MITRE ATT&CK group ID were found in the sources gathered. Bitdefender noted one technique resembling a feature of the 'FunnySwitch' backdoor linked to APT41, but called it an isolated similarity, so this record does not merge it with APT41 [S3]. Vendor name: Bitdefender. Most press coverage (SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Security Affairs, GovInfoSecurity) re-reports the single Bitdefender report and is not independent confirmation [S3][S4].

attribution.confidence: Bitdefender says the victimology points toward Chinese interests but the evidence is circumstantial; the origin and affiliation of the group are not confirmed [S1][S3]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Victim set concentrated on South China Sea government and military bodies, use of Gh0st RAT variants common among Chinese-speaking actors, and a single technique similar to the APT41-linked FunnySwitch backdoor that Bitdefender treats as isolated [S1][S3].

objectives: Bitdefender characterizes the activity as espionage against government and military organizations; exfiltration included browser data and messaging-app data [S1][S4]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered.

regions: South China Sea countries (individual countries not named in the sources gathered) [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: At least eight victims, mainly military and government, high-level organizations [S1][S3]. Bitdefender said the actor repeatedly regained access to the same entities through spear-phishing, and that exploitation reflected poor credential hygiene and inadequate patching of exposed devices and web services [S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access has been spear-phishing with archives (zip files containing LNK files) that lead to the SerialPktdoor backdoor; in March 2024 the archives were disguised as Microsoft Defender installers or themed on US political issues [S4]. Ps2dllLoader has been used since 2018 to load .NET agents such as SharpJSHandler and SerialPktdoor; from 2023 the actor shifted toward MSBuild.exe loading C# payloads from a remote SMB share, which Bitdefender describes as pushing Ps2dllLoader into a backseat role rather than retiring it [S1][S4]. Gh0st RAT variants include SilentGh0st and TranslucentGh0st (since at least 2018) and newer modular variants FluffyGh0st, EtherealGh0st and InsidiousGh0st [S1][S4]. Exfiltration used DustyExfilTool (TLS over TCP) initially, then curl over FTP with dynamically generated credentials (exact transition date not confirmed) [S1][S2]. Since at least September 2022 the actor used ITarian RMM to gain a foothold, which Bitdefender calls unusual for a state-linked actor [S1][S3]. Collection scripts targeted Chrome and Edge browser data, and samples show the actor terminating Telegram and Viber and archiving their data with rar.exe [S1][S4]. The original summary also cites scheduled tasks and local administrator account manipulation for persistence; these were not re-confirmed in the sources gathered [S5].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed, Chinese-aligned espionage actor per Bitdefender; no confirmed sponsor [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with LNK archives, SerialPktdoor, SharpJSHandler, Ps2dllLoader, MSBuild fileless loading, Gh0st RAT variants, ITarian RMM, DustyExfilTool and curl/FTP exfiltration [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Remote SMB share used to host C# payloads for MSBuild; FTP and TLS-over-TCP exfiltration servers [S1][S4]. Specific domains and IPs were not captured here.
diamond.victim: Government and military organizations in South China Sea countries, at least eight victims, repeatedly re-compromised [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: South China Sea regional government and military intelligence interest, consistent with Chinese interests per Bitdefender's circumstantial assessment [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached through email, plus exposed devices and web services with weak patching and credential hygiene [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is government and military email gateways and endpoints in South China Sea partner nations, plus exposed devices and web services with weak patching [S3]. STEP 2: The actor has persisted for years, re-compromised the same victims, and uses remote management tooling and fileless loading to blend in [S1][S3]. STEP 3: The template is spear-phish with zip/LNK, then SerialPktdoor or Gh0st RAT variant, then MSBuild or RMM footholds, then browser and messaging data collection and FTP/TLS exfiltration [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued intelligence collection against regional partner government and military networks. MDCOA is use of retained access during a regional crisis for deeper collection; this is judgment, not stated in sources. Candidate indicators: MSBuild.exe loading from remote SMB shares, unexpected ITarian RMM agents, curl FTP outbound transfers, rar.exe archiving of Telegram or Viber data, and LNK-in-zip attachments with Defender or US-politics lures [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: share MSBuild-from-SMB, unauthorized RMM and curl-FTP detections across partner networks, as victims are regional government and military bodies [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: partner-network hunting and sharing depends on coalition agreements; clarify before action. (3) Mission assurance: long dwell time and repeated re-entry mean eradication must include credential resets and patching of exposed services [S3]. (4) Coordination: route indicators through cyber-defense and partner liaison channels; treat attribution as unconfirmed [S1][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Unfading Sea Haze is a threat actor focused on espionage, targeting government and military organizations in the South China Sea region since 2018. They employ spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments to gain initial access, followed by the deployment of custom malware such as Gh0st RAT variants and SharpJSHandler. The group utilizes scheduled tasks and manipulates local administrator accounts for persistence, while also incorporating Remote Monitoring and Management tools into their attacks. Unfading Sea Haze demonstrates a sophisticated and patient approach, remaining undetected for years and showing adaptability through evolving exfiltration tactics and malware arsenal.
